c1.story:
Stand at the counter of any kirana for ten minutes and watch what leaves the shop. A loose cigarette, lit before the buyer has reached the door. A packet of Tata Tea. A pouch of Fortune oil. A bag of Aashirvaad atta. A pesticide bottle for the farmer who came in from the next village. Every one of those is filed under FMCG on your screener, and every one of them is a different business.

That is the trap with this label. The four doors above share a sales channel, the kirana and the distributor's van, but almost nothing else. The cigarette is a tax-collection business with a brand attached: the government sets most of the shelf price, the law bans new brands from advertising, and the incumbent keeps a margin no other consumer business in India can touch. The tea and the atta are brand-and-reach businesses: the margin is modest, and the game is getting a household to stop buying loose wheat from the chakki and start buying a sealed pack with a name on it. The cooking oil is, under the brand, a refining and trading business living on the gap between what palm oil costs at Kandla and what a pouch sells for. And the pesticide seller is really a farm business that happens to use the same dealer-and-credit model.

Why does this matter so much? Because the same headline lands in opposite ways. A good monsoon is a gift to the farm-input seller and the staples brand. An Indonesian palm-oil curb is a crisis for the refiner and a nuisance for the biscuit maker. A Union Budget tobacco hike is the whole year for ITC's cigarette arm and irrelevant to Tata Consumer.

In FMCG, the shelf is shared. The economics are not.

ITC is the classic straddler: Gold Flake on one side, Aashirvaad and Sunfeast on the other. Patanjali Foods, the old Ruchi Soya bought out of insolvency in 2019, is a branded-foods story sitting on top of an edible-oil refinery. AWL, the Fortune company that Adani exited in 2025, is the reverse: a refiner trying to become a brand. When you own one of these, you own the pieces, and the market will price each piece on its own clock.
c1.read:
The four tiles are the four doors. Read each from top to bottom, then compare the bars across all four.

  • The name and the line under it say how the money is made: a taxed, legally frozen cigarette market; a brand sold through distributors at a modest margin; a commodity spread; or a farm product sold on dealer credit.
  • The tickers are listed names that mostly sit behind that door. Click one to open its stock page. Notice ITC appears under two doors, which is the straddling point from the story.
  • The profit bar is the part to stare at. Tobacco sits at high, because the law and the habit freeze competition. Branded staples and farm-input sellers sit at medium, earned through reach and the season. Commodity processors sit at low, because a litre of refined palm oil is a litre of refined palm oil.
  • The last line is the bet you are actually making: the tax rate, distribution reach, a spread, or the sky.

The analogy below the tiles gives you a mental picture for each door, and the so-what line gives the one rule to remember: never compare margins across doors. A refiner with a thin margin is not a badly run cigarette company. Before you look at any ratio for an FMCG name, decide which tile its profit actually comes from, using the segment table in its annual report.

c2.story:
Follow a litre of cooking oil backwards from your kitchen and you get a map of the whole industry. It reached you from a kirana, or from a quick-commerce dark store ten minutes away. Before that it sat in a distributor's godown, delivered by a salesman who visits that shop every week. Before that it was branded, priced and advertised. Before that it was refined and packed at a plant near Kandla, Haldia or Kakinada. And before that it sailed in as crude palm oil from Indonesia or Malaysia.

That is the five-station kitchen, and almost every FMCG product walks through it. Tobacco leaf comes from regulated auctions where farmers sell their crop. Tea comes from auction floors and estates. Wheat comes from mandis. The second station turns those into something you can sell: leaf into cigarettes, crude oil into refined oil, wheat into atta, loose tea into a blend that tastes the same every morning.

Then comes the station that creates most of the value: the brand. Indian FMCG sells at fixed price points, the five-rupee and ten-rupee packs your hand reaches for without thinking. Picking that price, then engineering the pack to fit it, is half the craft. The fourth station is distribution, the least glamorous and most powerful part of the business. A national brand's moat is often not its recipe but its truck, the fact that its salesman reaches a village shop that a newcomer cannot afford to visit.

Here is the twist of the last few years. That fourth station used to be a private road owned by the brands and their appointed distributors. Now Reliance Retail, DMart, Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart stand there too, and they negotiate. A brand that once dictated terms to a distributor now has to bargain with a platform that also sells its rivals and, sometimes, its own private label.

And where do the listed names stand? In the middle, processing, packing and branding, buying a commodity from the left and selling through a channel on the right that is getting bolder.
c2.read:
Read the top row left to right, then the band row underneath it.

The five boxes are the stations, from the farm and the port on the left to the household on the right. Each box says what happens there and who stands there. Watch how the names change: farmers, auctions and foreign palm exporters on the left; ITC, Godfrey Phillips, AWL, Patanjali and Tata Consumer in the middle; distributors, Reliance Retail, DMart and the quick-commerce apps towards the right; a crore-plus kiranas at the end.

The band row says who holds each station. The coloured Indian-listed cells sit under stations two and three, processing and brand. That is the picture of the business: listed FMCG buys a commodity it cannot control and sells through a channel it increasingly does not own.

Notice what is missing. There is no second band row, because no foreign rival stands across this kitchen the way China does in chemicals. The threats here are domestic: the unbranded loose product, the channel that wants a bigger cut, and Reliance stepping into the brand station with lower prices.

Then read the note on geography. Edible-oil refineries cluster at the ports where palm oil lands, and roughly a third of sales come from rural India, so the cost line that matters is the distributor's truck. Use the diagram like a circuit: a palm-oil shock enters at station one and lands on station two's margin within weeks; a channel fight at station four shows up as higher trade discounts at station three.

c3.story:
FMCG has the widest customer base of any industry on this site: essentially every household in India. But not every customer moves the needle equally, and the one that decides most years is not the one you see in advertisements.

The swing customer is the rural household. In a normal year it buys sachets, small packs and a steadily growing share of branded staples. Its wallet depends on the monsoon, crop prices, rural wages and government transfers. When those are healthy, rural volume grows faster than urban, and the whole industry looks good. When they are not, as in 2022, when food inflation ate into budgets, the rural buyer did something rational and painful for the brands: it traded down to loose atta, local oil and unbranded tea. The household did not stop eating. It stopped paying for the logo.

The urban middle class is steadier but has its own mood swings. It buys the premium tea, the ready-to-cook pack and the branded oil, and it tracks salaries and IT hiring. When urban demand slowed in 2024 and 2025, the premium end of every portfolio felt it first.

Then come the odd customers. Smokers are the least price-sensitive buyers on the list right up until the tax moves, at which point the illicit stick becomes very tempting. Export buyers of rice, shrimp and sugar live at the mercy of Delhi: when India banned non-basmati white rice exports in July 2023, traders lost a market overnight, and got it back only when the ban was lifted in 2024.

And then there is the customer that is also a channel. Quick commerce and modern trade buy fast-moving packs and premium variants, but they also set prices, demand margins and push their own labels. They are customers that negotiate like competitors.

The rural household rarely stops eating. It stops paying for the logo.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group. Read every tile in three lines.

  • The name is who is buying.
  • The second line is what they buy: sachets, staples, cigarettes, bulk oil, pesticides, export rice, premium packs.
  • The third line is what moves them, which is your watch list outside the industry.

Now sort the tiles by what drives them. Rural households and farmers both run on the monsoon and crop prices, so they move together, and together they are the biggest swing. Urban households and restaurants run on salaries and eating-out habits. Smokers run on tax. Export buyers run on government notifications and global prices. Quick commerce runs on the platforms' own expansion and discounting.

That sort tells you something useful about each company. A staples brand selling mostly rural is a leveraged monsoon bet. A cigarette company is a tax bet with one tile. A rice exporter's fate can turn on a single DGFT notice. A brand winning on quick commerce may be winning share at a lower margin.

Then read the so-what line under the tiles: rural volume is the swing factor, and a good monsoon with firm crop prices shows up in FMCG volumes about two quarters later. That one line is why the monsoon map is on the desk of every consumer analyst in Mumbai from June to September.

c4.story:
Here is the cleanest way to see why investors pay so much for the best FMCG names: follow a hundred rupees of sales and watch how much survives.

Start with a cigarette. One quirk first. On the shelf, most of the price of a stick goes straight to the government as tax, so the company reports its sales net of that tax. On what is left, the leaf, the paper, the filter and the pack are cheap. Advertising is banned, so there is no ad war to fund. The plant is modest. What survives is more than half of every rupee of net sales, a margin that makes a software company look ordinary. This is why ITC's cigarette arm has funded its hotels, its paper business and its foods push for decades.

Now take a branded staple: a pack of atta, salt or tea. The wheat, the salt and the tea leaf are most of the cost, roughly six of every ten rupees. Then come the people who make it famous and the trucks that get it to a village: ads, trade schemes, distributor margins, salesmen. What survives is under a tenth. Respectable, steady, but no cash machine.

The interesting part is how these companies handle a cost spike. They rarely raise the price, because the price point is sacred: the ten-rupee pack must stay ten rupees. So they shrink the pack first, a few grams at a time. In 2022, when palm oil and wheat hit records, Indian shoppers got smaller biscuit packs, thinner soap bars and lighter pouches before they saw a higher sticker. Economists call it shrinkflation; brand managers call it grammage engineering.

When costs jump, the price stays put and the pack gets smaller. Watch the grams, not just the rupees.

One more line worth knowing: other income. ITC and the cash-rich names sit on large treasury balances, and the interest on that cash quietly props up profit growth in a slow year. Strip it out before you decide whether the core business grew.
c4.read:
The two bar charts walk a hundred rupees of sales down to what is left, one for tobacco and one for branded staples and foods. Start at the left of each and move right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees. For tobacco, think of it as net sales, after the excise the company collects for the government.
  • The input bar is raw materials and packaging. In the tobacco chart it takes only about a quarter. In the staples chart it takes roughly six of every ten rupees. That gap alone explains why the two doors live in different worlds.
  • The opex bar is ads, distribution and people. Staples spend more here, a bit over a quarter of sales, because a brand that cannot advertise loudly and reach a village shop does not stay a brand. Tobacco spends less than a fifth, because the law caps the ad war.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is a sliver in both. These are light plants and, for the big brands, no debt.
  • The last bar is what remains: more than half for tobacco, under a tenth for staples.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover a bar for the rupee amount.

Below the charts, the list marks which P&L lines matter. Gross margin, ad spend and tobacco tax get a clear yes. Working capital, capex and other income get a sometimes: the brands run on distributors' money, while processors carry inventory. Depreciation and interest get a no. The so-what line is the habit to build: split every quarter's growth into price and volume before you believe it.

c5.story:
FMCG is supposed to be the boring corner of the market, the place you hide when everything else is on fire. And it is, in the sense that people do not stop buying tea and oil. But the stocks have their own cycle, driven by two things: how many packs people buy, and what the ingredients cost.

The boom came with the pandemic. In 2020 and 2021 households pantry-loaded staples and packaged food, and FMCG became the market's safe haven. Cigarettes were the exception, hurt by lockdowns, and ITC spent those years as the stock everybody loved to call a value trap.

Then 2022 turned the cost line upside down. Russia invaded Ukraine, wheat and sunflower oil spiked, and in April Indonesia briefly banned palm-oil exports. Companies took record price hikes and shrank packs. Growth looked healthy on paper, but it was almost all price. That is the peak: revenue up, volumes quietly rolling over.

The bust followed fast. Rural buyers, squeezed by food inflation, traded down to loose products, and volumes fell outright. Commodity prices eased in 2023 and margins rebuilt, but the volume did not come back with them, and urban demand began slowing too. The stocks lagged the market through 2024 and into 2025, the bottom of the clock.

Then two policy shocks arrived in opposite directions. In September 2025 the GST Council moved most packaged foods to the lowest slab, a price cut the companies did not have to pay for, and volumes have responded. In February 2026 a new central excise on cigarettes replaced the old cess and landed as a steep tax increase. So the clock reads early volume recovery for foods and staples, with a fresh headwind for tobacco and rising palm oil and crude for everyone in the second half.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock is split into four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top. The years under each arc are when the last cycle passed through it: boom across 2020 and 2021, peak in 2022, bust from 2022 into 2023, bottom across 2024 and 2025. Notice how short the peak-to-bust gap is: the cost spike and the volume collapse happened almost in the same year. The arrow points just past the bottom, into the start of the boom arc, labelled early volume recovery. Hover an arc to read what defined it.

The timeline retells the cycle from 2019. The colours carry the tone. Notice that 2022 is coloured as a bust year even though revenue was rising: the colour follows volumes and margins, not the headline.

The four hands are the readings that move the arrow. Two point the right way and two the wrong way, which is exactly what early and uneven looks like.

  • Rural versus urban volume: rural ahead, up arrow. That is the classic shape of a broad recovery.
  • Palm oil and crude: rising, down arrow. Expect a gross-margin squeeze for a couple of quarters before price hikes catch up.
  • Cigarette tax: sharply higher, down arrow. Legal volumes will dip while the market absorbs it.
  • Price versus volume mix: volume led, up arrow. The healthy kind of growth.

The readings are as of when the explainer was written; the arrows show the last direction of travel.

c6.story:
An FMCG company's quarter is decided by a surprising cast of strangers. A palm planter in Sumatra. A trade official in Jakarta deciding whether to curb exports. A finance ministry official drafting the tobacco lines of the Union Budget. A meteorologist at the India Meteorological Department tracking the monsoon's onset over Kerala. A shopper in Lucknow deciding whether this month is a branded-atta month or a loose-atta month.

Four of these dials carry the full three-dot weight, and they pair up neatly. Food inflation and the monsoon set the volume line: inflation shrinks the household's room for branded products, while a good monsoon and firm rural wages expand it, with a lag of about two quarters. Palm oil and cigarette tax set the margin line: palm oil feeds the refiners, the snack makers and the soap factories in the sister industry, and the cigarette tax decides the price of every legal stick.

Then come the supporting dials. Crude oil matters more than you might think, because the laminate around every sachet and the diesel in every distributor's truck are oil products. The rupee cuts both ways: a weaker rupee makes imported palm and soybean oil dearer for AWL and Patanjali, and makes exported rice and shrimp more competitive for the traders. Government food export policy is the dial that can flip overnight: a wheat export ban in May 2022, a rice ban in July 2023.

Notice something about the arrows. Almost every dial hurts when it rises. That is what a defensive industry looks like from the inside: it does not need anything in the economy to boom. It needs costs and taxes to stay calm and the rain to arrive on time. FMCG is less a bet on growth than a bet on nothing going wrong.

FMCG does not need the economy to boom. It needs costs to stay calm and the rain to arrive on time.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: how it reaches the profit and loss statement. For FMCG the channels split into two families: household purchasing power, which drives volume, and input or tax cost, which drives margin.
  • A rise does: the effect of the dial going up. A green up arrow helps, a red down arrow hurts, and a diamond cuts both ways. Count them: only the monsoon and consumer non-durables output are green; the rupee is the lone diamond; everything else is red.
  • Weight: one to three dots. Four rows carry three dots here: food inflation, the monsoon, palm oil and cigarette tax.

The last column shows today's reading where a dial maps to a series we track: consumer food inflation, Brent crude, the rupee, factory output of consumer non-durables and the money-market rate. For the monsoon, the series shown is fertiliser output, a proxy for how hard farmers are sowing. Palm oil, cigarette tax and export policy show a dash; for those, follow the news and the companies' commentary.

Use the table in two passes. First read the three-dot rows and ask: which family is moving, volume or cost? Then check which door a company sits behind. A palm-oil spike is a three-dot event for AWL and a footnote for ITC; a tobacco hike is the reverse. The so-what line below gives the shortcut: food inflation and the monsoon, between them, set both lines.

c7.story:
FMCG looks like a business with no bottlenecks at all. There is no factory that takes five years to build, no licence auction, no scarce mineral. And yet the margins have a ceiling, and the stocks have tripped over the same few stones again and again.

The biggest stone is structural: India imports well over half its edible oil, mostly palm from Indonesia and Malaysia. That means a policy meeting in Jakarta can reshape Indian margins within weeks, as it did in April 2022 when Indonesia briefly halted palm-oil exports. Indian refiners cannot simply buy local; there is not enough domestic oilseed to go round.

The second is a habit that has become a constraint: fixed price points. Because the five- and ten-rupee packs are sacred, companies cannot pass on a cost spike cleanly. They shrink the pack instead, and shoppers notice. Shrink too far and the buyer switches to a loose alternative.

Then come the tobacco twins. Tax risk is recurring: one budget can reset volumes. And the illicit market is structural: smuggled and counterfeit cigarettes already take roughly a quarter of the market, and every tax hike widens the price gap that makes them attractive. The government's tax lever and the smuggler's opportunity are, in effect, the same lever.

The newer frictions are in the channel. Quick commerce and modern trade often sell below the kirana's price, and distributor associations have pushed back hard, complaining to the Competition Commission about quick-commerce pricing in 2024. A brand has to keep both its old distributors and its new platform partners happy, and they want opposite things.

And looming over everything is a slow burn: Reliance Consumer Products. Since relaunching Campa in 2023, Reliance has used its retail reach to sell drinks and staples at sharply lower prices. It will not break the incumbents in a quarter. It can grind their pricing power down over years.
c7.read:
Each row is one bottleneck, with why it bites and a severity label. The label tells you where the risk belongs in your thinking.

  • Structural: permanent. Edible-oil import dependence and the illicit cigarette market sit here. These cap margins across the whole cycle, so they belong in your valuation, not your news feed.
  • Recurring: comes back again and again. Fixed price points, tobacco tax and monsoon or food-policy shocks are here. These are the headlines that move a stock for a week or a quarter.
  • Cyclical: bites in bad times. Unbranded and regional rivals win share whenever inflation squeezes budgets, then lose it again when budgets recover.
  • Two-sided: cuts both ways. Channel conflict hurts brands that lean on quick commerce, but helps the ones with the strongest traditional distribution.
  • Slow: here it means a slow burn rather than a slow fix. Reliance's price war builds over years.

Read the table in pairs. The first pair, imports and price points, explains why branded staples margins rarely expand far: costs come from abroad and prices cannot move freely. The tobacco pair explains why every cigarette tax hike has a second, delayed cost in lost legal volume. The so-what line underneath tells you which ones deserve a news alert: tobacco tax and food export policy, because they arrive without warning.

c8.story:
In FMCG, the most important pricing decisions are often made by people who do not work at FMCG companies. Take the two biggest events of the last year, both of them signed in Delhi.

In September 2025 the GST Council moved most packaged foods to the lowest tax slab. Think about what that does. The company keeps its price before tax, the shelf price falls, and the shopper gets a cheaper pack the company did not pay for. Volumes follow. For a staples brand fighting loose products, a tax cut is a better weapon than any ad campaign.

Then in February 2026 a new central excise on cigarettes replaced the compensation cess that had sat on top of GST since 2017. The structure changed, and so did the burden: it landed as a steep increase. For ITC and Godfrey Phillips that is the single biggest variable of the year.

Some rules are quiet moats. COTPA, the 2003 tobacco law, bans tobacco advertising and mandates graphic warnings. It sounds like a burden, and it is one, but it also freezes the brand landscape: no newcomer can advertise its way into the market, so the incumbents keep their share. Legal Metrology rules force packs to print price, weight and unit price, which is why shrinkflation cannot stay hidden for long.

Other rules are switches. Customs duty on edible oil changes the landed cost and the refining margin within days: the government raised it in September 2024 to support oilseed farmers, then trimmed the duty on crude oils in 2025. DGFT export notices can open or shut the rice and sugar trades overnight.

And some rules are on the horizon. FSSAI has proposed front-of-pack labels warning about sugar, salt and fat. For a biscuit or snack brand, a warning on the front of the pack is a very different conversation from fine print on the back.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who it is, what it does, why you care, and its status. Use the status column to prioritise.

  • New: the GST Council's slab cut and the central excise on tobacco. These are the two that are moving numbers right now, in opposite directions: one lifts food volumes, the other dents cigarette volumes.
  • Live: actively in play. Edible-oil customs duty and DGFT export policy can change within a week; the Competition Commission's look at quick-commerce pricing could reshape how brands price across channels.
  • Always: permanent fixtures. COTPA, Legal Metrology, and pesticide registration with the fertiliser subsidy. They rarely make news, but they shape the field: COTPA freezes tobacco competition, Legal Metrology exposes pack-size tricks, and CIB&RC decides which molecules farm-input sellers may sell.
  • Coming: FSSAI's front-of-pack labelling. A slow risk for high-sugar, high-salt and high-fat products.

A useful habit is to map each row to the doors on card one. Tobacco answers to the excise and COTPA rows. Branded staples answer to GST, FSSAI and Legal Metrology. Processors answer to customs duty and DGFT. Farm-input sellers answer to CIB&RC. Dated regulatory news filtered for this industry sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Michael Porter's five forces boil down to one question: once the money comes in, who gets to keep it? Suppliers squeeze from one side, customers from the other, rivals fight for the same rupee, newcomers crowd in, and substitutes make the product unnecessary. FMCG gives you a near-perfect demonstration, because its two halves answer the question so differently.

Run cigarettes through the test. Rivalry is muted: the market is effectively a duopoly with a dominant leader. Suppliers are thousands of leaf farmers selling at regulated auctions, with little pricing power. Buyers are smokers, who do not haggle over their brand. Newcomers face a law that bans them from advertising, so they cannot build awareness. Almost every spoke says the same thing: the money stays with the incumbent.

Branded staples share some of that comfort. A family that has bought the same tea for twenty years is not shopping on price each week, and a national distribution network takes years to copy.

Now run edible-oil refiners, rice millers and seafood exporters through it. Rivalry is fierce, with dozens of players selling identical product. Suppliers are a handful of palm-exporting countries whose policy decisions set your cost. Buyers are wholesalers and foreign importers who will switch for a sliver of price. No wonder processors keep the least.

But the cigarette business has one spoke where it is weaker, and it is a big one: substitutes. Beedi, smuggled sticks and vapes all compete for the same habit. India banned e-cigarettes in 2019, but the illicit stick remains the real rival, and the government's own tax hikes keep making it more attractive. Cooking oil and rice have no such problem: there is no substitute for dinner.

Cigarettes win on four spokes and lose on one. The one they lose on is fed by the taxman.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure that force puts on the business. So a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: tobacco and brands, and commodity processors and traders. Look at the size first. The tobacco-and-brands shape is tucked close to the centre on rivalry, suppliers, buyers and entrants, mostly at one, with rivalry a touch higher. The processors' shape bulges out on the same spokes, at or near the outer ring on rivalry and pressing hard on suppliers and buyers. That contrast is the whole margin story from card four, drawn as geometry.

Then find the spoke where the shapes cross. On substitutes, tobacco reaches further than processors: illicit sticks, beedi and vaping threaten the habit, while nothing replaces cooking oil or rice. That crossing is the one weakness in an otherwise fortress-like shape, and it is the spoke that every tax hike enlarges.

The table beside the radar gives each score from zero, no pressure, to three, heavy pressure, with a one-line reason. Two ways to use it. For a branded staples name, mentally pull its shape slightly outward from tobacco on rivalry and entrants, since Reliance and regional brands press harder there. For a farm-input seller, add the monsoon as a hidden supplier: it is not on the radar, but it behaves like one. If you disagree with a reason for a company you own, redraw its shape; that is exactly how the framework is meant to be used.

c10.story:
An FMCG results call is a marathon of brand launches, channel commentary and celebrity campaigns. Most of it you can skip. Eight numbers tell you what actually happened, and the most important one is usually not printed in the results table at all.

That number is underlying volume growth: how many more packs the company sold, stripped of price hikes. Management usually says it out loud on the call or in the press release. It is the single best test of health. Revenue up with volumes down means the company is milking its brands. Revenue up on volumes means real demand.

Next is gross margin, the tug of war between input costs and pricing power. When palm oil or wheat spikes, it shows here first. Then EBITDA margin, which tells you what is left after ads and distribution, and which carries a trap: a company can protect it in a bad quarter by cutting ad spend. That is why advertising as a share of sales is on the list. A sharp ad cut in a weak quarter is a company borrowing from its future.

For the tobacco names there is a special number: cigarette volume growth. After a tax change, it tells you whether smokers are absorbing the higher price or drifting to illicit sticks. With the new excise landing in 2026, it is the one number the ITC and Godfrey Phillips calls will be judged on this year.

Finally, the housekeeping trio. Headline sales growth, to be split into price and volume. Inventory days, which flags either commodity stocking at a processor or channel stuffing at a brand pushing stock into distributors to flatter a quarter. And return on capital, which for the best brands is extraordinary, because they need so little capital to grow.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask of every company you own. Read the rows as a sequence: volume, then margin, then what the margin is hiding.
  • What good looks like is the benchmark, and here it often splits by door: brands and processors get separate marks for gross margin and return on capital, and cigarettes get their own mark for EBITDA margin. Always compare a company with the mark for its own door.
  • Today's industry median comes from the latest annual filings of the industry's listed companies in our database. It appears only for rows that map to a reported figure: gross margin, EBITDA margin, sales growth, inventory days and return on capital. Underlying volume, cigarette volume and ad share show a dash, because companies disclose them in commentary rather than in a standard line. You will have to listen for them on the call.

One caution specific to FMCG: the median blends four very different doors, from cigarette makers to oil refiners to pesticide sellers, so it can land in a place no real company sits. Treat it as a weather report for the whole label, not a benchmark for any one name. The better comparison is three-way: the company's own number, the good mark for its door, and its own trend over the last few quarters.

c11.story:
The best warnings about an FMCG quarter rarely come from the FMCG companies themselves. They come from the sky, the futures screen, the retail audit and the gazette.

The earliest voice is the monsoon. Rain and kharif sowing in July and August set rural incomes for the year, and those incomes show up in sachet and small-pack volumes about two quarters later. By the time a company tells you rural demand is strong, the monsoon map told you months ago.

A quarter ahead, a chorus speaks. Malaysian palm-oil futures reset edible-oil and snack input costs. Rural wage growth and payouts under the rural jobs scheme put cash in village pockets. Retail-audit trackers from Nielsen and Kantar count packs leaving shops before companies report them. Crude oil and packaging-film prices reset laminate and freight costs.

And then there are the same-quarter shocks: a tobacco line in the Union Budget, a DGFT export notification, and Hindustan Unilever's results. HUL is the bellwether. It reports early, sells everywhere and talks openly about demand, so the whole sector's narrative for a season is set on the afternoon HUL speaks.

Put the signals together and you get the rule. The industry is in a genuine up-cycle when volume growth is accelerating, rural is growing at least as fast as urban, and input costs are stable or falling. Today the first two are ticking: the GST cut is lifting packaged foods and rural has led for a year. The third is not: palm oil and crude are rising. Two out of three is an early recovery with a cost headwind, which is exactly what the call says. It leans towards branded staples and foods riding the GST cut, and stays cautious on tobacco until the new excise has worked through volumes.

The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot to read the channel through which it reaches earnings.

  • Far right, two quarters ahead: the monsoon and kharif sowing, alone. It is the earliest and most important signal on the chart.
  • The middle, one quarter ahead: palm-oil futures, rural wages and jobs-scheme payouts, the Nielsen and Kantar volume trackers, and crude with packaging film. Two of these are cost signals and two are volume signals, so check which way each pair is pointing.
  • Far left, the same quarter: tobacco tax decisions, export-policy notices and HUL's demand commentary. These do not warn you; they tell you what has just happened.

Use the chart as a reading order: the right-hand dot first, then confirm with the middle, then let the left-hand dots tell you whether the quarter has already turned.

Below the chart sits the three-sign rule. Two ticks: volume accelerating, with the note pointing to the GST cut, and rural matching urban, with rural ahead for a year. One cross: input costs, with palm oil and crude rising. Count the ticks against the rule above them: two of three reads as early recovery.

The call box gives the view, its three supporting points, and what would change it: a failed monsoon, a palm-oil spike from an Indonesian curb or a weak rupee, and a deeper Reliance price war. Treat those three as your alerts; if one appears in the news, the call is due for a rethink.
